shared_text:
The flight. A narrow-body airliner on a passenger flight, approaching to land in visual conditions.

The crew. The captain was the pilot flying; the other pilot was the pilot monitoring.

What happened. Arriving from the east, the crew planned a visual approach to the runway advertised on the ATIS, backed up by the ILS. The captain had planned only for that runway. The captain was surprised when approach control asked whether they preferred a localizer or RNAV approach to another runway. Asked about the planned runway, the controller said a drone was at 200 ft over its approach end and the other runway was now in use. The captain wanted the RNAV approach's vertical guidance but did not think there was time to set it up. The aircraft's speed and height suited an extended right downwind for the original runway; it was now on a high right base for the new one. The captain accepted the localizer approach and began setting up and briefing it while trying to lose height and speed before turning inbound. The captain felt rushed but did not ask for delay vectors. Trying to make the approach work, the captain did not note the distance from the final approach fix to the threshold. For the rest of the approach, speed and configuration met neither the captain's planned criteria nor the stabilised approach criteria; at the time, the captain did not realise the extent of this. The crew continued the approach and landed.
safe_outcome: The landing was uneventful. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: The aircraft could not be stopped on the remaining runway. It left the end of the runway at about 30 knots and came to rest on the grass. The passengers were evacuated, and two received minor injuries during the evacuation. The aircraft was slightly damaged.
notes: Removed under rule 3: the reporter's later characterisations 'anchored' (rendered as the observable fact that the captain had planned only for that runway), 'that was my first mistake', 'for some reason', 'this oversight negated my stabilized approach plan' and 'behind the aircraft', and the gate debrief and resolution to take delay vectors or go around in future. 'I failed to note' is rendered 'did not note'. Kept as said or felt at the time: surprise at the controller's question, the wish for the RNAV vertical guidance and the belief that there was no time to set it up, feeling rushed, and the aim to 'make it work'. Kept as a fact stated afterwards, with the captain's state at the time: speed and configuration outside the planned and the stabilised approach criteria, and the captain not realising the extent until after landing (the 'after landing' is left out because it refers to the outcome). Moved under rule 5: 'uneventful landing'. Removed under rule 6: the runway identifiers (the planned runway and 'another runway'). Judgement calls: 'end', because the unstable state was speed and configuration carried from a high, fast base to landing; the standard safe-ending sentence is used because the drone was over the other runway's approach end and the report shows no conflict between this aircraft and any traffic, only the runway change, which is in the shared text. The other pilot is called 'the other pilot' because the report does not name their role.
